q: 1. For a sub-merged curved surface, the horizontal component of force due to static liquid is equal to
options: weight to liquid supported by the curved surface
force on a projection of the curved surface on a vertical plane
area of curved surface × pressure at the centroid
explain: The horizontal component of hydrostatic force on a curved surface is equal to the force exerted on the vertical projection of that curved surface.

q: 2. For a sub-merged curved surface, the component of force due to static liquid is equal to
options: weight of the liquid supported by curved surface
force on a projection of the curved surface on a vertical plane
area of curved surface × pressure at the centroid
explain: The vertical component of hydrostatic force on a curved surface is equal to the weight of the liquid vertically above the curved surface up to the free surface.

q: 3. An oil of specific gravity 0.7 and pressure 0.14 kgf/cm² will have the height of oil as
explain: Pressure P = ρgh. Converting 0.14 kgf/cm² to kgf/m² gives 1400. Density of oil = 0.7 × 1000 = 700 kg/m³. Height h = 1400 / 700 = 2 meters.

q: 4. The velocity of pressure wave in terms of bulk modulus (K) and density (ρ) is given by
explain: The speed of sound or a pressure wave in a fluid is determined by the fluid's compressibility (Bulk Modulus, K) and its mass density (ρ), calculated as C = √(K/ρ).

q: 5. Euler's number is the ratio of
explain: Euler's number (Eu) expresses the relationship between the inertia force and the pressure force in a fluid flow.

q: 6. Froude's number (Fe) is given by
explain: Froude's number is defined as the ratio of inertia force to gravity force, mathematically expressed as Fr = V / √(gL).

q: 7. The square root of the ratio of inertia force to gravity force is called
explain: The Froude number represents the square root of (Inertia Force / Gravity Force), commonly used in open channel flow and wave studies.

q: 8. The square root of the ratio of inertia force to force due to compressibility is known as
explain: The Mach number is the square root of the ratio of the inertia force to the force due to compressibility (elastic force).

q: 9. The square root of the ratio of inertia force to pressure force is known as
explain: The Euler number is the square root of the ratio of the inertia force to the pressure force.

q: 10. Model analysis of aeroplanes and projectile moving at super-sonic speed are based on
explain: For high-speed flows where compressibility effects are significant (supersonic), the Mach number is the primary similarity parameter used for model testing.

q: 11. Drag is defined as the force exerted by a flowing fluid on a solid body
options: perpendicular to the direction of flow
in the direction which is at an angle of 45°
explain: Drag is the component of the total force exerted by the fluid on the body in the direction of the relative motion (parallel to the flow).

q: 12. Total drag on a body is the sum of
explain: Total drag consists of skin friction drag (viscous resistance) and pressure drag (form drag due to pressure differences between the front and back of the body).

q: 13. A body is called bluff body if the surface of the body
options: does not coincide with the streamlines
explain: A bluff body has a shape that does not coincide with streamlines, causing flow separation and a large wake, resulting in high pressure drag.

q: 14. Terminal velocity of a falling body is equal to
options: the maximum velocity with which body will fall
the maximum constant velocity with which body will fall
explain: Terminal velocity is reached when the sum of the drag force and buoyancy equals the downward force of gravity, resulting in zero acceleration and constant velocity.

q: 15. When a falling body has attained terminal velocity, the weight of the body is equal to
options: drag force plus the buoyant force
explain: At equilibrium (terminal velocity), the downward Weight (W) is balanced by the upward forces: Drag (Fd) and Buoyancy (Fb). Thus, W = Fd + Fb.

q: 16. The boundary-layer takes place
options: for flow over flat plate only
explain: Boundary layers form in 'real' (viscous) fluids due to the no-slip condition at the solid boundary. Ideal fluids have no viscosity and thus no boundary layer.

q: 17. The boundary layer is called turbulent boundary layer if
explain: For flow over a flat plate, the transition from laminar to turbulent boundary layer typically occurs at a critical Reynolds number of approximately 5 × 10⁵.

q: 18. Laminar sub-layer exists in
explain: Even in a turbulent boundary layer, there is a very thin region extremely close to the wall where viscous forces dominate and the flow remains laminar; this is the laminar sub-layer.

q: 19. The separation of boundary layer takes place in case of
explain: Boundary layer separation occurs in the presence of an adverse (positive) pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0), where the fluid is moving against increasing pressure.

q: 20. The drag force exerted by a fluid on a body immersed in the fluid is due to
explain: Drag is the combined effect of shear stress (viscous force) and the pressure distribution (pressure force) acting on the surface of the body.

q: 21. Super-sonic flow means
explain: Supersonic flow is defined as flow where the speed of the fluid exceeds the local speed of sound, resulting in a Mach number greater than 1.

q: 22. Sonic-flow means
explain: Sonic flow occurs when the fluid velocity is exactly equal to the local speed of sound (Mach = 1).

q: 23. In sonic-flow, the disturbances, created by a projectile, moves
explain: In sonic flow, the projectile and the pressure disturbances it creates travel at the same speed, so they move together.

q: 24. In super-sonic flow, the projectile (which creates disturbances) moves
explain: In supersonic flow, the projectile travels faster than the speed of sound (the speed of disturbances), so it stays ahead of the pressure waves it creates.

q: 25. For sub-sonic flow, if the area of flow increases
explain: In subsonic flow (Mach < 1), a diffuser (increasing area) causes the velocity to decrease and the pressure to increase, as per the continuity and Bernoulli principles.

q: 26. For super-sonic flow, if the area of flow increases, then
explain: In supersonic flow (Mach > 1), the relationship between area and velocity is inverted: an increase in area actually causes an increase in velocity.

q: 27. Numerical value of gauge pressure is
explain: Absolute Pressure = Gauge Pressure + Atmospheric Pressure. Therefore, gauge pressure is always less than absolute pressure by the amount of atmospheric pressure.

q: 28. For a supersonic flow, velocity increases
options: with the decrease of area of flow
with the increase of area of flow
when area of flow is constant
explain: As noted in question 495, for supersonic flow (Mach > 1), the velocity increases as the cross-sectional area of flow increases.
